summary: This ResearchGate-hosted article by Leon Balter (The Psychoanalytic Quarterly, 2018, vol. 66(4):619-645) describes the Nicholas Young phenomenon, in which dreams shift immediately to more regressive mental functioning whenever the dreamer or protagonist crosses a topographical boundary or threshold in the manifest content. The abstract presents eight examples and explains the phenomenon through dreams in series, Scherner's Law on their sequential trend toward regression, and Silberer's 'symbolism of the threshold' linked to the mind's self-observing capacity. The page also lists related Balter papers on nested dreams and works of art, plus an unrelated 1995 article on the written dream.
one_line: Balter's 2018 Psychoanalytic Quarterly article on the Nicholas Young phenomenon, where crossing a threshold in dreams triggers more regressive mental functioning.
key_facts: The article 'Spatial Translation and Regression in Dreams: The Nicholas Young Phenomenon' was published in August 2018.
It appeared in volume 66, issue 4, on pages 619-645, with DOI 10.1177/0003065118797137.
The sole listed author is Leon Balter.

The Nicholas Young phenomenon involves an immediate shift in dreams to more regressive mental functioning whenever the dreamer or protagonist crosses a topographical boundary or threshold in the manifest ideational content.
The phenomenon is also called spatial translation in the abstract.
The phenomenon furthers the regression typical in dreams.
The abstract presents eight examples of the Young phenomenon.
The explanation addresses dreams in series, or dream sections in series.
The explanation refers to Scherner's Law, which covers the sequential trend toward regression in dreams in series.
Silberer's 'symbolism of the threshold' is invoked to explain the spatial translation of the Young phenomenon.
The explanation refers to the mind's self-observing capacity.
